To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
visuospatial WM processes are reflected in fNIRS hemodynamic responses and that these responses are sensitive to mental-ability-induced individual differences in the brain.
fNIRS is a sensitive method to measure visuospatial WM-related brain activation and that this activation is modulated by mental ability.
fNIRS is sensitive for detecting visuospatial WM-related functional activation in the pre- frontal cortex and that this activation is reduced for participants with far above-average mental ability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an fNIRS-based assessment tool for visuospatial WM processes in children.
the development of an fNIRS-based method for the assessment of WM-related functional activation in the pre-frontal cortex in children.
the question how fNIRS data can be interpreted in the context of visuospatial WM.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sensitivity and mental-ability-induced functional activation differences of the visuospatial WM task as measured by fNIRS were successfully confirmed in children.
the sensitivity of fNIR spectroscopy to visuospatial working-memory-specific task demands is not only valid for young adults but also for 11- to13-year-old children.

fNIRS recordings are sensitive for identifying functional hemodynamic brain changes related to visuospatial working-memory processing and that these hemodynamic changes are differentially expressed in children with different mental abilities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
visuospatial WM performance in children can be assessed with fNIRS.
fNIRS recordings are sensitive to visuospatial working-memory-related brain activation in both children and young adults.
fNIRS recordings are sensitive to identify WM-related functional brain activation in both children and young adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fNIRS recordings are a valid tool to study functional activation in the pre-frontal cortex during WM processing, especially when combined with mental ability as a moderator.

fNIRS is a sensitive tool for identifying functional brain activation during visuospatial WM processes, and that mental-ability-induced changes in functional activation can be reliably detected in children.

fNIRS is a promising tool for studying visuospatial WM processes in children and that it can be used to identify differences in the functional organization of visuospatial WM in children with high and low mental ability.
